skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development

skills.name: test-development

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

36. ///
37. /// # Description
38. ///
39. /// A type that represents a physical address.
40. ///
41. #[verus_verify(external_derive)]
42. #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
43. pub struct PhysicalAddress(VirtualAddress);
44. 
45. //==================================================================================================
46. // Implementations
47. //==================================================================================================
48. 
49. impl PhysicalAddress {
50.     pub fn from_virtual_address(addr: VirtualAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
51.         // Delegate to the per-platform validator to support sparse physical memory layouts.
52.         if !crate::hal::platform::is_valid_physical_address(addr) {
53.             return Err(Error::new(
54.                 ErrorCode::BadAddress,
55.                 "address out of bounds of physical memory",
56.             ));
57.         }
58. 
59.         Ok(Self(addr))
60.     }
61. 
62.     ///
63.     /// # Description
64.     ///
65.     /// Constructs a physical address from a memory-mapped I/O address.
66.     ///
67.     /// # Parameters
68.     ///
69.     /// - `addr`: The memory-mapped I/O address.
70.     ///
71.     /// # Return Values
72.     ///
73.     /// Upon success, a physical address associated with the given memory-mapped I/O address is
74.     /// returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
75.     ///
76.     /// # Safety
77.     ///
78.     /// Behavior is undefined if the provided memory-mapped I/O address is invalid.
79.     ///
80.     pub unsafe fn from_mmio_address(addr: VirtualAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
81.         Ok(Self(addr))
82.     }
83. 
84.     pub fn into_virtual_address(self) -> VirtualAddress {
85.         self.0
86.     }
87. 
88.     ///
89.     /// # Description
90.     ///
91.     /// Constructs a [`PhysicalAddress`] from a [`FrameNumber`].
92.     ///
93.     /// # Parameters
94.     ///
95.     /// - `frame`: The frame number.
96.     ///
97.     /// # Returns
98.     ///
99.     /// A [`PhysicalAddress`] associated with the given `frame_number`.
100.     ///
101.     pub fn from_number(frame: FrameNumber) -> Self {
102.         let addr: usize = frame.into_raw_value() * mem::FRAME_SIZE;
103.         Self(VirtualAddress::new(addr))
104.     }
105. 
106.     pub fn into_frame_number(self) -> FrameNumber {
107.         let raw_addr: usize = self.0.into_raw_value();
108.         let frame_number: usize = raw_addr >> mem::FRAME_SHIFT;
109.         // Safety: the following unwrap is safe because a physical address has a valid frame number.
110.         FrameNumber::from_raw_value(frame_number).unwrap()
111.     }

115.     ///

121.     ///
122.     /// # Returns
123.     ///
124.     /// A [`PhysicalAddress`] associated with the given `frame_addr`.
125.     ///
126.     pub fn from_frame_address(frame_addr: FrameAddress) -> Self {
127.         let raw_addr: usize = frame_addr.into_raw_value() << mem::FRAME_SHIFT;
128.         Self(VirtualAddress::new(raw_addr))
129.     }
130. 
131.     pub fn from_into_frame_address(frame_addr: FrameAddress) -> Self {
132.         let raw_addr: usize = frame_addr.into_raw_value() << mem::FRAME_SHIFT;
133.         Self(VirtualAddress::new(raw_addr))
134.     }
135. }

138.     ///
139.     /// # Description
140.     ///
141.     /// Instantiates a new [`PhysicalAddress`] from a raw value.
142.     ///
143.     /// # Parameters
144.     ///
145.     /// - `raw_addr`: The raw value.
146.     ///
147.     /// # Returns
148.     ///
149.     /// - `Ok(Self)`: The new address.
150.     /// - `Err(Error::BadAddress)`: If the provided address is invalid.
151.     ///
152.     fn from_raw_value(value: usize) -> Result<Self, Error> {
153.         Self::from_virtual_address(VirtualAddress::from_raw_value(value))
154.     }
155. 
156.     ///
157.     /// # Description
158.     ///
159.     ///  Aligns the target [`PhysicalAddress`] to the provided `alignment`. If the address is already

161.     ///
162.     /// # Parameters
163.     ///
164.     /// - `alignment`: The alignment to align the target address to.
165.     ///
166.     /// # Returns
167.     ///

169.     ///

171.         let aligned: VirtualAddress = self.0.align_up(align).ok_or_else(|| {
172.             let reason: &str = "align_up overflow";
173.             error!(

181.     }

 > Scope: design the abstract `View` (+ `inv`) for `PhysicalAddress` that the

 >

 > that skeleton against the caller analysis, applies the substitution test to
 > each candidate field, and designs the `inv()` and the spec transitions the
 > in-scope contracts will use.
 
 ---
 
 ## Abstract Resource
 
 `PhysicalAddress` is, to its callers, **an opaque integer identifier for a single
 byte location in guest-physical memory** — a validated handle whose only
 observable state is one mathematical integer, the **raw physical address**.
 
 It is the currency exchanged between the frame allocator (`mm/phys/frame.rs`),
 the paging / boot-init code (`mm/virt/boot_init.rs`, `mm/phys/mod.rs`), kernel
 module descriptors (`kmod.rs`), and the frame-granular wrappers
 (`PageAligned<PhysicalAddress>`, `FrameAddress`). From that single integer every
 caller derives the one further concept it ever needs: the **frame** the address
 lies in (`addr >> FRAME_SHIFT == addr / FRAME_SIZE`), used to index bitmaps and
 refcount arrays and to encode PTE/PDE frame fields.
 
 It is **not** a collection, resource manager, or state machine: it is an
 immutable, `Copy`, totally-ordered scalar value whose equality and ordering agree
 with integer equality/ordering of the raw address. That it is internally a
 newtype over `VirtualAddress` is invisible to callers — the caller analysis is
 explicit: callers "don't care that the inner representation is a `VirtualAddress`
 newtype … they go through `into_raw_value` / `into_virtual_address` / frame
 conversions."
 
 ---
 
 ## View Struct
 
 The abstract state of a `PhysicalAddress` is **exactly one value**: the raw
 numeric address as an unbounded integer. Verus models this with a scalar `View`
 (`type V = int`), not a one-field record, because there is only one
 caller-observable quantity. The existing inline skeleton is **kept unchanged**:
 
 ```rust
 impl View for PhysicalAddress {
     type V = int;
 
     // `closed`: callers may reference `self@`, but the mapping to the inner
     // VirtualAddress field is hidden. The abstract value is "the physical
     // address as an unbounded integer".
     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
         self.0@      // newtype identity: delegate to the inner address's view
     }

 ```

 tower — `VirtualAddress@ : int`, `PageAligned<T>@ : int`, `FrameAddress@ : int`,
 `FrameNumber@ : int` — confirming the abstraction is caller-driven, not
 implementation-driven: every member models a value as a single `int`.
 
 `view()` is **`closed`** so the newtype delegation (`self.0@`) does not leak the
 `VirtualAddress` representation; callers still obtain a usable `int` (`p@`) for
 arithmetic, frame indexing, and comparison.
 
 ### Equivalent "single-field" reading
 
 ```rust
 pub struct PhysicalAddressView {
     // addr: the numeric physical address this handle denotes, as `int`.
     //       The only state a caller can observe. The "frame it lies in" is a
     //       *derived* quantity (addr / FRAME_SIZE), not a stored field;
     //       in-range-ness is a *property* of this value, expressed by inv().
     addr: int,
 }
 ```

 The frame index is the single derived quantity callers reason about, so it gets a
 named helper over the abstract `int` rather than a stored field:
 
 ```rust
 // The frame that this physical address belongs to. Equals the implementation's
 // `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT`, stated as exact integer division so the spec is
 // independent of shift-vs-divide.
 pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
     addr_view / spec_page_size()
 }
 ```

 `FRAME_SIZE == spec_page_size()`). `spec_max_frame_number() : int` denotes
 `FrameNumber::MAX` (`= MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1`); together with

 `FrameNumber` type at the `phys.spec.rs` edge, and they are the vocabulary the
 `from_number` / `into_frame_number` contracts use.
 
 ---

 `PhysicalAddress` carries **one** universal property that every constructible
 value satisfies and that callers depend on: its address has a **representable
 frame number**. This is exactly the fact that makes `into_frame_number` total —
 its internal `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(addr >> FRAME_SHIFT).unwrap()` never

   inventing a failure condition the implementation does not exhibit.
 
 ### `PhysicalAddress` (the type)  *(in scope)*
 
 The type-level contract is precisely `inv()`: any `PhysicalAddress` value
 produced by a verified constructor satisfies
 `spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()`, and every in-scope
 operation returning a `PhysicalAddress` preserves it. Holding the type is the
 proof token that `into_frame_number` cannot panic; callers never re-check the
 bound.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Rationale (substitution test per item)
 
 > Test: *"If the implementation were completely rewritten with a different
 > algorithm, would this still make sense?"*
 
 | Item | Meaning | Substitution test |
 |------|---------|-------------------|
 | `self@ : int` (raw address) | The numeric physical address the handle denotes. | **Passes.** Whether `PhysicalAddress` is a newtype over `VirtualAddress`, a bare `usize`, or a struct with tag bits, "the integer physical address" is the one quantity every caller reasons about — frame indexing, ordering, equality, MMIO identity, raw round-trips. The `closed` view hides *how* the int is stored. |
 | `spec_frame_number(self@)` (derived helper) | The frame the address lies in. | **Passes.** Derived purely from `self@` and the module constant; any implementation that means "frame number" by `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` computes `addr / FRAME_SIZE`, regardless of shift-vs-divide. Not stored, so no rewrite can desync it. |

2. name: verus-constraints
3. description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Verus Constraints
7. 
8. ## Attribute Style for Exec Functions
9. 
10. All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
11. (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
12. See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.
13. 
14. ```rust
15. // ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
16. #[verus_spec(ret =>
17.     requires x < 100,
18.     ensures ret == x + 1,
19. )]
20. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
21.     x + 1
22. }
23. 
24. // ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
25. verus! {
26.     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
27.         requires x < 100,
28.         ensures ret == x + 1,
29.     { x + 1 }
30. } // verus!
31. ```
32. 
33. **`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
34. - `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
35. - Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)
36. 
37. Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
38. signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.
39. 
40. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
41. 
42. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
43. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
44. 
45. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
46. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
47. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
48. minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
49. 
50. **Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
51. comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.
52.

2. name: spec-design
3. description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Design Guide
7. 
8. ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
9. 
10. ### Qualities of a Good Spec
11. 
12. 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
13.    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
14.    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
15. 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
16.    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
17.    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.
19. 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,

250.   verified function with no additional logic.

252. ### Property Coverage Checklist
253. 
254. When writing specs, systematically cover these four dimensions for each
255. function and type. This ensures no important properties are missed.
256. 
257. 1. **Functional Correctness** — What does the code achieve?
258.    - Preconditions (requires): what must the caller guarantee?
259.    - Success postconditions (ensures, Ok case): new abstract state, return value, frame condition
260.    - Error postconditions (ensures, Err case): state preservation, failure condition in abstract terms
261. 
262. 2. **Safety** — What must never happen?
263.    - Bounds, disjointness, uniqueness, conservation, injectivity, ordering, monotonicity
264. 
265. 3. **Liveness** — What good things must happen?
266.    - Guaranteed success conditions, resource availability, recoverability
267. 
268. 4. **Structural Consistency** — Is the data self-consistent?
269.    - Type invariants, field relationships, valid ranges
270.

272.

274. 
275. - **Type invariant (`inv()`)** — defined on the View type (see **view-design**
276.   skill). Every constructor must establish it; every method must preserve it.
277.   If a property appears in `requires` of nearly every method, it belongs in
278.   `inv()` instead.
279. - **Loop invariant** — defined on loops. Must hold on entry (base case),
280.   be preserved by each iteration (inductive step), and together with the
281.   exit condition imply the function's `ensures` (sufficiency). Define

288.

290. verification?

293. (e.g., index bounds derived from loop invariants, capacity checked before
294. insertion). The runtime check serves as a safeguard during development;
295. once all callers are verified, it becomes dead code and can be removed.
296.

298. dynamic information (external input, hardware state, concurrent
299. operations) that no amount of static reasoning can discharge. A
300. `requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.
301.

303. runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
304. `// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
305. verification work knows to clean it up.

311. find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

315.    it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.

411. 
412. ### False Limitations (AI often thinks these are blockers, but they aren't)
413. 
414. | "Limitation" AI claims | Reality |
415. |---|---|
416. | "Can't verify generic types" | Verus has full generic support with type bounds |
417. | "Can't handle &mut parameters" | &mut params are fine; only *returning* &mut is blocked |

# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_physical_memory_regions` — iterates a std
  `alloc::collections::LinkedList` via `for region in list.iter()`. The build
  toolchain's `vstd` (`/mnt/toolchain/verus/vstd`) ships ghost-iterator specs only
  for `slice`/`vec`/`VecDeque`/`BTree*`/`Hash*` iterators, **not** `LinkedList`, and
  the orphan rule forbids supplying `View`/`ForLoopGhostIterator` impls for the
  foreign `linked_list::Iter` from the `kernel` crate (E0117). Genuine Verus
  front-end limitation, not a proof gap or code bug — full analysis in
  `verus-unsupported.md`. The abstract booking effect is specified over
  `PhysMemView` and discharged (no `admit`) by
  `lemma_book_region_reserves_region_frames` in `mod.proof.rs`. `ensures` keeps the
  caller-relevant guarantee: allocator stays initialized and well-formed.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/mod.rs::book_mmio_regions` — same std-`LinkedList`
  iteration limitation as above. Abstract effect (skip-if-not-covered; book tracked
  frames) discharged by `lemma_book_mmio_skip_untracked` /
  `lemma_book_mmio_books_tracked`. `ensures` keeps allocator initialized and
  well-formed across booking.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## Skip / exclude from current proof target

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/manager.rs::PhysMemoryManager::get_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::init`

## Allowed `external_body` — frame allocator core (`frame.rs`)

`frame.rs` is now the proof target. Two layers form the trust boundary of the
global frame-allocator singleton; everything else in the module (the `frame::*`
free-function shims) is **body-verified** against these contracts.

### 1. The singleton bridge: `instance()`

`instance()` returns `&'static mut Inner` obtained from the module-level
`static mut INSTANCE` via `unsafe { INSTANCE.assume_init_mut() }`. The verifier
does not support `static mut` paths, and a zero-argument uninterpreted
`phys_view()` cannot be tied to that static by any verifiable means. `instance()`
is therefore the bridge axiom: `requires phys_view().initialized` (the real panic
gate) and `ensures (*result).inv() && (*result)@ == phys_view().frames`. This is
what lets the query shims (`is_covered`, `refcount`) be fully body-verified.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — `static mut` singleton accessor;
  bridges the live `Inner` to the abstract `phys_view().frames`.

### 2. The `Inner::*` methods

Each `Inner::*` method has a rich, do-not-modify `old(self)@ → final(self)@`
transition contract, but its **body** cannot be translated by Verus: every method
uses the `error!` / `debug_assert_eq!` macros (whose expansion needs
`core::fmt::Arguments`, unsupported — the same limitation already recorded for
`UserFrame::drop`) and the `arch` newtypes `FrameNumber` / `FrameAddress`
(external types with no `external_type_specification`). They are `external_body`
with their pre-existing `#[verus_spec]` contracts honored as trust boundaries.

- `Inner::alloc`, `Inner::alloc_contiguous`, `Inner::free`, `Inner::share`,
  `Inner::refcount`, `Inner::book`, `Inner::is_covered`, `Inner::alloc_range`
  (all in `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs`).

### Note on the body-verified shims

The `frame::*` free-function shims are no longer `external_body`. The pure-query
shims `is_covered` and `refcount` are proven outright via the `instance()` bridge.
The aggregate query shim `free_count` is also fully body-verified via
`lemma_free_count` (`frame.proof.rs`): it counts the clear bitmap indices as the
image of an injective `i -> i * page_size` map and discharges
`free_frames.len() + usage == num_bits` without any `admit()`.

The mutating reservation shims (`alloc`, `alloc_contiguous`, `book`,
`alloc_range`, `share`) are body-verified and carry the **strong** post-state
contract via the `tracked PhysAuth` carrier threaded through `&mut`: each names
both `old(auth)@` (pre-state) and `final(auth)@` (post-state) and asserts the
exact `FrameAllocView` transition (`spec_alloc_one` / `spec_alloc_set` /
`spec_share`), with a meaningful `Err` arm (`final(auth)@ == old(auth)@`). They
carry no `admit()`.

## Allowed `external_body` — `frame::free` (`frame.rs`, `Drop` path)

`frame::free` is reached only from `UserFrame::drop` / `KernelFrame::drop`. Their
trait-fixed `drop(&mut self)` signature is `opens_invariants none` + `no_unwind`,
so the `Drop` path **cannot** receive a `Tracked<&mut PhysAuth>` carrier and
**cannot** open a global invariant to reach the authority. Without the token the
body cannot discharge `instance()`'s `phys_view().initialized` precondition nor
`Inner::free`'s `frame.inv()` precondition, and the contract must stay
precondition-free for `Drop` soundness. The function is therefore `external_body`
with its weak, always-true `ensures phys_view().inv()` honored as a trust boundary
(the logging branch performs no state change). This replaces the previous deferred
`proof! { admit(); }`; the trust surface is identical, but `external_body` is the
governed mechanism. It is the single deliberate, caller-justified `Drop`-path
exception — **not** the forbidden weakening, which concerned the reservation ops
that now carry the strong `PhysAuth`-threaded post-state.

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::free` — releases one reference on `Drop`.
  `ensures phys_view().inv()` on every path; no precondition (`Drop`-safe).

## Allowed `external_body` — `UserFrame::drop` (`upool.rs`)

32.

34.     /// # Description
35.     ///

37.     ///

41.     ///
42.     /// # Returns
43.     ///
44.     /// - `Some(`[`FrameNumber`]`)`: Upon success.

76.     /// # Safety
77.     ///
78.     /// Behavior is undefined if the provided memory-mapped I/O address is invalid.
79.     ///
80.     // Deliberately bypasses the RAM-range validity check (MMIO GPAs may lie
81.     // outside tracked RAM). On success it is pure identity wrapping
82.     // (`r@ == addr@`); the `unsafe` contract — that `addr` denotes a valid MMIO
83.     // frame — is encoded as `requires` (frame-representability) so the result
84.     // satisfies the type invariant and may later flow into `into_frame_number`.

86.         requires
87.             spec_frame_number(addr@) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
88.         ensures
89.             match result {

91.                 Err(_) => true,

116.     // Alignment (`result@ % FRAME_SIZE == 0`) and the type invariant follow from
117.     // this value relation, so they are not listed separately.
118.     #[verus_spec(result =>
119.         ensures
120.             result@ == spec_from_number(spec_frame_raw_value(frame)),

123.         proof! { admit(); }

6. // A `PhysicalAddress` abstracts to a single mathematical integer: the raw

18. // canonical frame size, re-exported from `crate::hal::mem` (defined alongside

26. // `FrameNumber` lives in the `arch` crate, which is not Verus-enabled and has no

28. // external datatype so it may appear in spec-fn parameters and the
29. // `assume_specification`s below. Its internals are not modeled (`external_body`):
30. // its abstract index is projected by `spec_frame_raw_value`.

40. // prescribes. `spec_max_frame_number()` denotes `FrameNumber::MAX`.

55. 
56. // The base (frame-aligned) address of a frame index: `frame * FRAME_SIZE`.
57. pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
58.     frame_view * spec_page_size()
59. }
60. 
61. // ── `arch`/`sys` library-edge `assume_specification`s ─────────────────────────
62. 
63. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE` is the frame size (alias of `PAGE_SIZE`), tied to the
64. // canonical `spec_page_size()`.
65. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE ] -> (result: usize)
66.     ensures
67.         result == spec_page_size(),
68. ;
69. 
70. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT == log2(FRAME_SIZE)`. Bounded below the pointer width
71. // so `raw_addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` is well-defined.
72. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT ] -> (result: usize)
73.     ensures
74.         result < usize::BITS,
75. ;
76. 
77. // `VirtualAddress::new` is a pure newtype constructor: the wrapped value is the
78. // abstract address. (`sys` library edge; the inner module is not yet verified.)
79. pub assume_specification[ VirtualAddress::new ](value: usize) -> (result: VirtualAddress)
80.     ensures
81.         result@ == value as int,
82. ;
83. 
84. // `<VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value` is pure newtype identity: the
85. // returned raw `usize` equals the abstract address.
86. pub assume_specification[ <VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value ](
87.     addr: VirtualAddress,
88. ) -> (result: usize)
89.     ensures
90.         result as int == addr@,
91. ;
92. 
93. // `FrameNumber::into_raw_value` projects a frame number to its index; every
94. // `FrameNumber` value is in range (`0 ..= MAX`) by construction.
95. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::into_raw_value ](frame: FrameNumber) -> (result: usize)
96.     ensures
97.         result as int == spec_frame_raw_value(frame),
98.         0 <= spec_frame_raw_value(frame) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
99. ;
100. 
101. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value` succeeds iff `value <= MAX`, preserving the index.
102. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::from_raw_value ](value: usize) -> (result: Option<FrameNumber>)
103.     ensures
104.         match result {
105.             Some(f) => value as int <= spec_max_frame_number()
106.                 && spec_frame_raw_value(f) == value as int,
107.             None => value as int > spec_max_frame_number(),
108.         },
109. ;
110. 
111. // ── Type invariant ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
112. //
113. // Every `PhysicalAddress` a verified constructor produces has a *representable
114. // frame number*: `self@ / FRAME_SIZE <= FrameNumber::MAX`. This is the load-
115. // bearing fact that makes `into_frame_number` total (its internal
116. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never panics), which the frame
117. // allocator relies on when using the result directly as a bitmap / refcount
118. // index. It is *not* alignment (MMIO addresses may be unaligned) and *not*
119. // RAM-validity (`from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses that check).
120. impl PhysicalAddress {
121.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
122.         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
123.     }
124. }
125. 
126. } // verus!
127.
